name: Test Doubles and Over-Mocking
intent: Replace slow or unsafe collaborators with the right kind of test double, and keep the tests tied to what the code does rather than to how it does it, so green does not mean wrong in production.
scenario: An order service reserves stock and charges a payment gateway, releasing the stock if the card is declined. The team tests it with stubs, strict mocks, mocks of everything, fakes and a contract test, then hits the service with 6 real bugs and 2 harmless refactors to see which suites notice.
problem: Test double is the umbrella word for anything that stands in for a real collaborator: a dummy only fills a parameter and is never used, a stub returns canned answers, a mock records and verifies calls, a spy records calls for later checking, a fake is a simple working version, such as an in-memory database. The usual advice is to isolate the unit by replacing its dependencies, and the trap is how far that goes. A test that replaces everything and asserts that certain calls happened checks the script of the implementation, not the result. It passes while production fails, because the double encodes what the author believes the real thing does, and it fails on a harmless refactor, because the calls changed. Practitioners disagree on mocks and fakes: mockists favour interaction tests and fast design feedback, classicists favour state tests and real or fake collaborators. Each side pays for its choice somewhere.

howItWorks.title: Name the kind of double you need
howItWorks.text: A stub answers questions with canned values, so the code under test can proceed. A mock expects specific calls and fails the test if they do not happen. A spy records what happened so the test can check afterwards. A fake is a lightweight implementation that really works, such as an in-memory repository that keeps state and enforces rules. Choosing the kind decides what the test can learn.

howItWorks.title: Prefer asserting on outcomes
howItWorks.text: A test that places an order and then checks the charged amount and the remaining stock survives many refactors, since any way of reaching that state passes. A test that checks that reserve was called once and charge twice breaks when the implementation changes the order of calls, even when the behaviour is the same.

howItWorks.title: Mock where the interaction is the behaviour
howItWorks.text: Some behaviour is only a call: send an email, publish an event, charge a card exactly once. There an interaction check is the honest assertion, because the call is what matters. Use mocks at those edges, and keep them off internal helpers and values.

howItWorks.title: Make your fakes match the real contract
howItWorks.text: A hand-written fake is only as true as its author's memory of the real service. If the real gateway starts requiring a key, the fake still says yes. Run a small contract test against the real service or its sandbox, and keep the fake honest by running the same checks against both.

howItWorks.title: Check that the test can fail
howItWorks.text: After writing a test, break the production code on purpose, for example swap two arguments, and make sure the test goes red. A test that cannot fail is documentation at best. Counting what a suite catches and what it breaks on a refactor tells you more than counting tests.

pros: Fast, deterministic tests that never call real payment or email services
Easy to force rare cases: a declined card, a timeout, an out-of-stock item
Interaction checks pin down behaviour that is only a call, such as exactly one charge
Fakes give realistic behaviour without the cost of the real dependency
cons: A double only knows what its author knew, so it can pass while the real service differs
Strict interaction tests fail on refactors that keep the behaviour, which makes people stop refactoring or stop trusting the tests
A realistic fake is code you must write and keep in step with the real service
Lots of setup per test hides what the test is about and makes it hard to read
whenToUse: A collaborator is slow, costs money, sends real messages or is hard to put into a rare state
The behaviour under test is an outgoing call, such as publishing an event or charging a card once
A fake of a stable, well-understood dependency can be shared by many tests
whenNotToUse: To replace your own simple helpers and value objects, where the real one is just as easy to use
As the only check on an integration: doubles cannot tell you that the real parts fit
To assert the exact order of internal calls that nobody outside the class depends on
pitfalls: Stubs with canned answers and tests that assert only the returned status: all tests pass, and in the model 0 of 6 bugs are caught
Strict mocks that assert every internal call: 5 of 6 bugs caught, but both harmless refactors break the suite
Mocking so much, including your own calculator, that the test checks the mocks and not the code
A fake that follows an old contract, so the missing key or changed rule passes in tests and fails in production
Verifying calls that cannot fail, because the double returns what the test expects
Skipping a contract test or a few integration tests because the unit tests are green

roles.label: Test

roles.label: Test double
roles.description: A stub, mock or fake standing in for a collaborator.

roles.label: Real gateway
roles.description: The real payment service, with rules the double may not know.

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: Writes the tests and refactors the service.

quiz.question: A suite uses a stub that always answers success, and every test asserts only the returned status. What does a green run tell you?
options: That the service handles payment errors, because tests passed.
Almost nothing about charging, since the stub cannot reveal a wrong amount or missing release.
That the real gateway accepts the service's calls.
That the service is safe to refactor.
quiz.explanation: A stub that always says yes checks only that the code reaches the end. Wrong amounts, missing stock releases or bad arguments do not change the returned status, so they pass.

quiz.question: After a harmless refactor that adds one extra stock lookup, 40 tests fail. Each one verifies the exact list of calls. What does that point to?
options: The tests are tied to how the service works, not to what it does.
The refactor changed the behaviour and the tests rightly caught it.
The stock lookup should be removed, since the tests expected otherwise.
Mocks are always wrong and should never be used.
quiz.explanation: The behaviour was the same: the same charge and the same stock. Strict interaction checks pin the implementation, so they break on refactors. Mocks are still the right tool where the call itself is the behaviour.

quiz.question: The real gateway now requires an idempotency key. Tests using an older hand-written fake still pass. How can the team catch this?
options: Add more assertions to the fake tests.
Replace the fake with a stub that returns success.
Run a small contract test against the real sandbox, and check the fake against the same cases.
quiz.explanation: Only the real service knows its own rules. A contract test against the sandbox fails on the missing key, and sharing its cases with the fake keeps the fake honest. A stricter mock still encodes the old belief.
